The post Arizona boy faces rare oral cancer with help from proton beam therapy close to home appeared first on Mayo Clinic News Network. ]]> When Jake Garcia was 7 years old, a routine visit to the dentist led to a diagnosis his family never expected: a rare oral cancer.
Jake would need surgery, chemotherapy and radiation therapy. Through a collaboration between Mayo Clinic and Phoenix Children's Hospital, Jake received proton beam therapy at Mayo Clinic, home to Arizona's only proton beam therapy program.
Watch: Jakey's story
Journalists: Broadcast-quality video (2:31) is in the downloads at the end of this post. Please courtesy: "Mayo Clinic News Network." Read the script.
Proton beam therapy delivers radiation directly to a tumor while reducing radiation exposure to surrounding healthy tissue, a precision that is especially important for children.
"For pediatric cancers, we strongly favor proton beam for almost any site simply because of that principle of reducing overall exposure to radiotherapy in a developing child, where we want to cure the cancer while avoiding potential longer-term developmental side effects or risks of other cancers in the future," says Dr. Jonathan Ashman, medical director of the Proton Beam Therapy Program at Mayo Clinic in Arizona.
The benefits extend beyond pediatric care; in a study published in The Lancet, Dr. Samir Patel, a radiation oncologist, and investigators found that patients with head and neck cancers can live longer with fewer side effects if treated with proton beam radiation therapy.
Jake and his twin sister, Ella Garcia
Cancer affects more than the patient.
Throughout his cancer journey, his family worked to preserve as much normalcy as possible for Jake and his twin sister, Ella. Having proton beam therapy available in Phoenix allowed the family to stay close to home during treatment and maintain important routines.
Mayo Clinic's Child Life team also helped Jake and Ella navigate an experience that could be frightening and unfamiliar. For Jake, comfort sometimes came in the form of Seaweed, his stuffed turtle, who accompanied him to treatment. Seaweed even inspired the ocean scene painted on Jake's radiation mask.
Elizabeth Hardin, child life specialist, with Jake
Ella faced the experience alongside her twin brother. A child life specialist helped her better understand why Jake needed treatment and what was happening to him, an important part of supporting the entire family through a child's cancer diagnosis.
Jake also held onto the things he loved. He continued drawing and creating comics and kept up with karate during his cancer journey.
Today, he is back in school, spending time with friends, drawing and just earned his black belt in karate.
Jake, Ella and part of his care team at Mayo Clinic in Arizona

The post Mayo Clinic research offers new way to understand memory and neurodegenerative disease appeared first on Mayo Clinic News Network. ]]> Dr. David T. Jones reviews brain scans on a computer at Mayo Clinic.
ROCHESTER, Minn. — A new framework, published in Brain, could reshape researchers' understanding of how the brain creates memories and experiences, and how disruptions in this process may indicate Alzheimer’s disease and other forms of dementia.
David T. Jones, M.D., a Mayo Clinic neurologist and director of the Mayo Clinic Biological Intelligence Lab, and his collaborator, Michael Breakspear, M.B.B.S., Ph.D., of the University of Newcastle in Australia, have mapped out how the brain's limbic system processes and organizes information using a concept from generative artificial intelligence (AI) called latent diffusion.
In generative AI models, latent diffusion engines convert complex information, such as an image or text prompt, into a compressed representation of its underlying features. The model then processes that information within a latent, or hidden, space before converting it back into an output.
Their proposed framework, called stochastic latent oscillatory diffusion (SLOD), breaks latent diffusion across inner brain structures into four core processes: compression, diffusion, conditioning and decompression.
"We propose the hippocampus doesn't store memories the way a filing cabinet stores documents. Instead, it learns the underlying features of the world and models it at a deeper level," says Dr. Jones, likening it to a creative engine. "The format that it's using is so flexible that the hidden features of the world can be combined and produced into new things beyond what you know or have experienced."
The framework grew in part from a problem Dr. Jones encountered while treating a memory-loss syndrome impacting the brain's limbic system called limbic-predominant amnestic neurodegenerative syndrome, or LANS.
TDP-43, the protein associated with LANS, often accumulates in the brains of people with the syndrome. While caring for patients with LANS, Dr. Jones observed that sometimes TDP-43 was absent, and when it was present, it often occurred alongside other protein abnormalities.
"I simply could not wrap my head around it," he recalls. "If this is all occurring in the limbic system, where several brain structures converge, protein buildups may be telling us where the problem is rather than being the whole of the problem."
How the proposed memory framework works
The cerebral cortex, the part of the brain that processes cortical information, such as sensory, cognitive and internal stimuli, is where SLOD begins. The stimuli are compressed and travel to the hippocampus via the entorhinal cortex, a major pathway to the inner brain.
Once the stimuli reach the hippocampus, they undergo diffusion and denoising. Underlying representations of the stimuli are conditioned there until the brain has a need to recall or reconstruct them, such as for memory or even imagined memory, for output back through connected brain structures.
This research also presents new avenues to identifying neurodegenerative dementias, proposing that disruptions to the four diffusion processes might help physician-scientists classify neurodegenerative diseases, rather than relying solely on cellular or protein abnormalities. For example, a brain’s failure to compress stimuli may be indicative of Alzheimer’s disease, Dr. Jones explains.
Although SLOD is theoretical, Dr. Jones remains optimistic about its potential impact.
"This research opens up a whole new way to approach cures, and that is exciting. Why wouldn't we want new avenues to treat dementia?" he says. "This is just the beginning."

ROCHESTER, Minn. — Mayo Clinic researchers, in a study published in Nature Communications, have identified a group of BRCA2 gene variants associated with a moderate risk of breast cancer, a finding that could help healthcare teams better assess a person's cancer risk and personalize care.
The researchers studied 70 BRCA2 gene variants, that they labeled as hypomorphic variants because they only partially disrupt BRCA2 function. They examined how these variants affect the way BRCA2 works and analyzed genetic testing data from a large number of people who had undergone hereditary cancer testing.
Researchers within the study note that individuals who inherit these specific gene changes are estimated to have a 20% to 25% lifetime risk of developing breast cancer. By comparison, people with more common harmful BRCA2 variants may have a 50% to 70% lifetime risk. Because of this reduced risk, these variants are also labeled as reduced penetrance pathogenic variants.
Fergus Couch, Ph.D.
"This shows that not all harmful BRCA2 variants carry the same level of breast cancer risk," says Fergus Couch, Ph.D., a breast cancer researcher at Mayo Clinic Comprehensive Cancer Center. "Understanding these differences could help us better match cancer prevention and screening strategies to an individual's actual risk."
The findings have potential implications for cancer screening and prevention. The researchers note that people who carry these variants may still qualify for and benefit from regular mammograms and breast MRI. However, a more precise understanding of risk could be important when patients and their healthcare teams consider risk-reducing surgery.
"A small subset of breast cancers are likely caused by BRCA2 hypomorphs," says Dr. Couch. "Women and men who inherit these variants should benefit from risk management strategies tailored to the level of risk associated with the specific variant."
The researchers also examined whether tumors associated with these variants may be sensitive to PARP inhibitors, a class of targeted cancer drugs that interfere with the ability of cancer cells to repair damaged DNA.
Their findings suggest that some of the tumors associated with hypomorphic BRCA2 variants may respond to PARP inhibitors. Tumor testing may help determine whether this type of treatment is appropriate for an individual patient.
The researchers are continuing to identify and characterize hypomorphic variants in the BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes associated with inherited breast cancer risk.
"Once the hypomorphic variants are all identified, we will be able to better define risk management and therapeutic strategies for those who carry these variants," Dr. Couch says.
The research was conducted in collaboration with investigators from Ambry Genetics. For a full list of funding, disclosures and contributing authors, see the study.

ROCHESTER, Minn. — A blood biomarker for Alzheimer's disease may help estimate a cognitively healthy person's risk of developing mild cognitive impairment or dementia over the next five or 10 years, according to a new Mayo Clinic study in JAMA Neurology.
The approach combines a blood measure of phosphorylated Tau 217 (p-tau217), a biomarker associated with Alzheimer's disease, with age, sex and genetic risk to estimate a person's future risk of cognitive impairment. Higher p-tau217 levels and older age were associated with greater risk.
Alicia Algeciras-Schimnich, Ph.D.
"The goal is to provide a personalized estimate of the risk of developing cognitive impairment that is more meaningful than simply reporting whether a blood test is positive or negative for amyloid pathology," says Alicia Algeciras-Schimnich, Ph.D., a Mayo Clinic laboratory medicine and pathology researcher and first author of the study.
Building on earlier risk-prediction research
The study builds on previous Mayo Clinic research that used PET brain scans to measure amyloid, a protein that accumulates in the brain in Alzheimer's disease, and predicts future cognitive impairment. The new work applies a similar approach using a blood biomarker, which is less invasive and potentially more scalable.
Researchers analyzed 1,644 cognitively unimpaired participants in the Mayo Clinic Study of Aging and 534 participants in the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative. Participants were ages 60 to 90 and had p-tau217 blood measurements, genetic testing and repeated cognitive assessments over time.
Using the Mayo Clinic Study of Aging data, researchers estimated the likelihood of developing mild cognitive impairment (MCI) or dementia within five and 10 years. They then used the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative data to confirm the association between higher p-tau217 levels and greater risk of cognitive decline.
For example, a 75-year-old woman who did not carry APOE e4, a common genetic risk variant for Alzheimer's disease, had an estimated five-year risk of MCI of 5% with a relatively low p-tau217 level and 16% with a higher level. Her estimated 10-year risk rose from 12% to 35%.
Age made a substantial difference as well. At the same high p-tau217 level, the estimated five-year MCI risk ranged from 6% at age 65 to 37% at age 85.
Putting risk into a clinical context
The findings could become especially relevant if therapies now being studied can prevent or delay cognitive decline before symptoms appear.
Ronald Petersen, M.D., Ph.D.
"A person may want to know: What is my risk of developing cognitive impairment in the next five or 10 years, and how does this blood test change that risk?" says Ronald Petersen, M.D., Ph.D., a Mayo Clinic neurologist and director of the Mayo Clinic Study of Aging. "If preventive therapies prove effective, those numbers could become very important in treatment decisions."
Ongoing prevention trials, including AHEAD 3-45 and TRAILBLAZER-ALZ 3, are testing whether amyloid-targeting therapies can delay cognitive decline before symptoms appear. Both used blood biomarkers to help identify participants, underscoring the potential role of tests such as p-tau217 in earlier stages of Alzheimer's disease.
Clifford Jack, Jr., M.D.
"Absolute risk gives the biomarker result clinical context," says Clifford Jack Jr., M.D., a Mayo Clinic neuroradiologist and senior author of the study. "If preventive treatments become available, this kind of information could help patients and clinicians have more informed conversations about the potential benefits and risks of treatment."
The researchers note that the risk estimates were developed in the Mayo Clinic Study of Aging and will need further study in more diverse populations and with other p-tau217 blood tests. Alzheimer's biomarker testing is not currently recommended for people without cognitive symptoms.
For a complete list of authors, disclosures and funding, review the study.

ROCHESTER, Minn. — Mayo Clinic researchers developed and tested an artificial intelligence (AI) model that used results from a standard 24-hour urine test to predict kidney stone composition more accurately than a conventional urine-based calculation. Using the AI model, researchers correctly predicted kidney stone composition in 73% of patients, compared with 33% using the conventional calculation alone.
The findings, published in Mayo Clinic Proceedings, could provide doctors and other healthcare professionals with another source of clinical information when a kidney stone is not available for testing. Knowing what a stone is made of can help guide treatment and prevention strategies. The model is intended to supplement, not replace, existing test results and trends.
"Many patients never have a kidney stone available for analysis, so doctors are often working with an incomplete picture," says Patrick Day, senior author of the study and a principal developer in Mayo Clinic's Department of Laboratory Medicine and Pathology. "Our findings show that AI may help us get more clinically useful information from a test that is already part of kidney stone care. For patients, that could mean more informed treatment decisions. For laboratories and healthcare systems, it highlights how existing laboratory test data can be used in new ways to support clinical care."
The study's first author, Eric B. Lantz, Ph.D., a senior data science analyst in Mayo Clinic's Department of Laboratory Medicine and Pathology, developed the AI model using data from more than 13,000 patients, including age, sex and results from 24-hour urine tests. The researchers then evaluated the model using data from 1,653 additional patients.
Stone composition can help guide treatment
Kidney stones are common and can be very painful. One in 11 Americans will have a stone at least once in their life, and the lifetime recurrence rate is high at 60% to 80%. Most kidney stones are made of calcium oxalate, though calcium phosphate and uric acid stones are also common.
Identifying the type of stone can help doctors determine treatment and strategies to reduce the risk of another stone. The most direct way to determine composition is to analyze the stone itself, but a stone is not always available. Patients may not collect the stones they pass, and stones may not be available for testing after surgery. In those cases, doctors may rely on clinical information and laboratory results to estimate the stone's composition.
Finding more information in a standard test
The 24-hour urine test measures substances in the urine that can contribute to kidney stones. The test can help identify a patient's risk factors and guide treatment, but it produces many individual measurements, and the relationships among them can be challenging to interpret.
The researchers developed the AI model to analyze those measurements together, identify patterns and predict the most likely kidney stone type. The study found the model performed better than the conventional calculation alone, including when researchers looked at different age and sex groups.
"Laboratory tests contain useful information not only in the individual results but also in the relationships among them," says Dr. Lantz. "AI can identify those patterns and could help us get more clinical value from data we are already collecting."

ROCHESTER, Minn. — Awake deep brain stimulation (DBS) surgery can provide information beyond what imaging alone can capture, helping clinicians personalize electrode placement for patients with essential tremor, according to a Mayo Clinic study published in Operative Neurosurgery.
DBS surgery involves implanting thin wires with electrodes, known as leads, into specific areas of the brain. The electrodes deliver electrical impulses that affect brain activity and can be used to treat brain disorders such as essential tremor, Parkinson's disease and dystonia. Imaging helps clinicians plan where to place the leads.
"In many patients, following a standard target based on imaging can lead to optimal therapy. But sometimes the best lead location for a patient may be in a slightly different position," says Bryan Klassen, M.D., a Mayo Clinic neurologist and study co-author.
During awake DBS surgery, neurosurgeons and neurologists can measure brain activity, test stimulation and receive feedback from the patient. This information can help the surgical team adjust lead placements during the procedure.
"It is an interactive process that gives us the ability to evaluate patient responses during the procedure and immediately adjust lead placement if neurophysiological recordings or stimulation testing reveal suboptimal positioning," says Matthew R. Baker, Ph.D., a neurosurgery scientist at Mayo Clinic and study co-author. In contrast, DBS performed while the patient is asleep relies primarily on imaging to guide lead placement.
In the retrospective study, Mayo Clinic researchers examined 137 DBS leads implanted in patients who were awake during surgery for essential tremor. Researchers evaluated how often information gathered during surgery changed the final lead position and whether those changes could have been achieved using imaging alone.
Workflow for comparing planned and final lead placement
A. The preoperative planning CT was aligned with the postoperative CT to identify the final DBS lead position. B. The planned trajectory and final lead position are shown after alignment. C. The final lead position (yellow star) was compared with the imaging-defined target (red circle) and planned trajectory (blue circle) to determine whether the lead moved closer to, farther from or remained the same distance from the target. In this example, the lead was moved anteriorly, away from the planned target.
For each lead, researchers determined whether the final implant followed the planned path, required an adjustment in depth, or was moved to a parallel path based on recordings of brain activity and stimulation testing. They also compared tremor suppression and side effects before and after leads were repositioned.
About 15% of the 137 leads were meaningfully repositioned. Among those adjustments, 88% could not have been achieved through imaging-based corrections alone.
"The awake procedure frequently led to lead adjustments that would not have been made if clinicians had relied solely on imaging during asleep procedures," says Dr. Klassen. "This is evidence that awake surgery enables a more individualized and optimized lead placement strategy for each patient, increasing the likelihood that a patient receives the best possible therapeutic outcome."
During surgery, repositioned leads also produced more favorable responses, including better tremor control, fewer side effects and wider therapeutic windows — the range between the stimulation level needed to control symptoms and the level at which side effects emerge.
"A wide window provides greater flexibility during future programming and improves long-term treatment management," says Dr. Klassen.
The findings suggest that awake testing can provide clinically useful information even as imaging and surgical technologies advance. Researchers note that clinicians cannot reliably determine before surgery which patients will need the additional information provided by awake testing.
"What this study shows is that when we do make those adjustments, they are often based on information that imaging alone could not provide. That gives us another way to personalize treatment for the individual patient," says Kai Miller, M.D., Ph.D., a Mayo Clinic neurosurgeon and study co-author.
The team is studying ways to make awake DBS procedures more efficient while preserving patient-specific information. Future research includes developing technologies that can evaluate multiple measures of brain activity simultaneously, as well as new patient tasks, stimulation approaches and targeting strategies.
"The next step is to find ways to gather this information more efficiently," Dr. Miller says. "Our goal is to shorten the procedure while preserving the information that helps us make better decisions for each patient. As we learn more about neural biomarkers and develop better tools to measure them, we may be able to further refine how we personalize DBS treatment."
The research supports Mayo Clinic's Bioelectronics Neuromodulation Innovation to Cure (BIONIC) initiative, which seeks to develop personalized neuromodulation therapies to prevent, treat and potentially reverse neurological disorders.
For a complete list of authors, disclosures and funding, review the study published in Operative Neurosurgery, an official publication of the Congress of Neurological Surgeons published by Wolters Kluwer Health.

PHOENIX — Radiation therapy is sometimes needed after mastectomy and breast reconstruction for breast cancer. However, patients with implant-based reconstruction who receive radiation therapy have a higher risk of capsular contracture, a complication in which scar tissue tightens around the implant. In more severe cases, it can cause breast pain, firmness, or distortion and may require additional surgery.
A Mayo Clinic study published in the International Journal of Radiation Oncology, Biology, Physics found that areas around the implant receiving both higher proton beam radiation doses and elevated linear energy transfer (LET) were associated with capsular contracture. LET measures how densely protons deposit energy as they travel through tissue. If validated in larger studies, the findings could help clinicians refine proton therapy plans to reduce the risk of this complication.
"Pencil beam scanning proton therapy can deliver precise doses of radiation for breast cancer while sparing healthy tissue and organs in the chest," says Wei Liu, Ph.D., research director of medical physics at Mayo Clinic in Arizona and co-senior author of the study. "These findings give us a possible direction for making an already precise treatment even safer."
The retrospective study reviewed data from 145 patients at Mayo Clinic who received pencil beam scanning proton therapy for breast cancer. Eight patients developed clinically significant capsular contracture. Researchers compared their treatment plans with those of 16 carefully matched patients who did not develop the complication.
"We found that patients who developed capsular contracture tended to have more small areas where moderate or high radiation doses overlapped with elevated LET," says Dr. Liu. "Our findings suggest that it may not be enough to evaluate radiation dose or LET separately during radiation therapy planning, but rather the combination and overlap should be considered."
The research is part of the Mayo Clinic Comprehensive Cancer Center's Novel Therapeutics and Therapeutic Modalities Research Program, which includes research on proton therapy and strategies to reduce treatment toxicity. Dr. Liu is a member of the program. Robert Mutter, M.D., a breast radiation oncologist at Mayo Clinic in Rochester, Minnesota, and co-senior author of the study, co-leads the program.
"Proton therapy gives us extraordinary control over where radiation dose is deposited, but dose alone may not tell the whole story," says Dr. Mutter. "At Mayo Clinic, we routinely consider linear energy transfer when designing proton treatment plans, particularly where beams stop near sensitive normal tissues. These findings reinforce the importance of considering dose and LET together and may help us refine how we optimize proton therapy moving forward."
Next, the research team plans to validate the findings in larger groups of patients across multiple institutions and further evaluate the dose-LET relationships identified in this study. The team also will investigate whether incorporating LET into proton treatment planning can reduce normal tissue exposure to unfavorable combinations of dose and LET while preserving treatment effectiveness and sparing nearby organs.

Shennen Mao, M.D., left, works with collaborators as they prepare a donor kidney for research in Mayo Clinic’s Organ Rejuvenation Unit in Florida.
Mayo Clinic researchers are keeping donor organs functioning outside the body longer, creating time to study damage, test treatments and potentially restore more organs for transplant.
In front of Mayo Clinic transplant surgeon Dr. Shennen Mao, a human kidney functions outside the body, connected by tubing to a perfusion machine that keeps it active.
Warm, oxygenated fluid moves through the organ's blood vessels. The kidney filters waste from the circulating fluid and produces urine, carrying out some of the same work it would do inside a patient.
The kidney arrived at Mayo Clinic's Organ Rejuvenation Unit in Florida after transplant centers nationwide deemed it unsuitable for transplant because of disease, injury or poor function.
Under perfusion, Dr. Mao and her team can watch how the kidney responds and test whether treatments can improve its function, with the goal of making more donor kidneys available for transplant.
"One of the hardest things as a transplant surgeon is seeing patients become too sick for transplantation and knowing that, if an organ were available, we could help them," says Dr. Mao, surgical director for Kidney Transplant and Living Kidney Donation at Mayo Clinic in Florida. "This work is about making more organs available and getting them to patients sooner."
More than 800 people are waiting for kidney transplants at Mayo Clinic in Florida, which performed 227 kidney transplants in 2025. Nationwide, more than 95,000 people are waiting for a kidney, according to the Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network. Yet nearly 30% of deceased donor kidneys recovered for transplant in 2024 ultimately were not transplanted.
How could longer organ perfusion make more kidneys transplantable?
Dr. Shennen Mao
Dr. Mao and her team, including Dr. Eduardo Chini, Dr. Sonu Kashyap, and Dr. Fouad Chebib, can currently keep donor kidneys functioning outside the body for hours. The researchers want to extend that window to as long as 21 days, creating more time to test treatments, track how an organ responds, and determine whether its function can be improved for transplantation.
"We're really just scratching the surface of what we can do with perfusion and how we can make organs better," Dr. Mao says. "We're working to breathe new life into these kidneys."
A longer window could be especially useful for kidneys that are difficult to transplant because of age or disease, including kidneys from donors older than 75 and those from donors with diabetes or high blood pressure.
"If we can support these kidneys through the process of transplantation, stabilize them, and put them into a healthy environment, they can likely give years of good kidney health to their recipient," Dr. Mao says.
Keeping a diseased kidney functioning also gives researchers a chance to see what is happening inside the organ.
The team recently completed its first perfusion of a kidney affected by polycystic kidney disease, which causes cysts to grow throughout the organ and can lead to kidney failure. With the kidney still functioning outside the body, researchers were able to study how the disease affects its physiology and metabolism in real time.
Testing new ways to protect and repair donor kidneys
For much of transplant history, transplant teams kept donor kidneys cold before surgery. Cooling slows an organ's metabolism and limits damage. Cold machine perfusion later allowed teams to pump fluid through the kidney, but the organ's metabolic activity remained greatly reduced.
Normothermic perfusion keeps the kidney at body temperature and metabolically active, giving researchers new opportunities to intervene. Because the kidney is isolated from the rest of the body, Dr. Mao and her team can test interventions directly on the organ without exposing a patient to an experimental treatment. They also are studying whether changes to the preservation fluid could keep the kidney stable longer.
The team also is studying the immune response that can lead to rejection. One approach, known as "immunologic cloaking," could modify a donor kidney before transplant so the recipient's immune system is less likely to recognize it as foreign. Dr. Mao hopes the approach could expand options for highly sensitized patients and reduce immune-related damage after transplant.
Longer perfusion also could give researchers time to test regenerative treatments, including cell-based therapies designed to repair damaged tissue.
Shennen Mao, M.D., left, and collaborators monitor and evaluate a donor kidney during a perfusion experiment in Mayo Clinic’s Organ Rejuvenation Unit in Florida.
The challenge is applying those treatments across an entire kidney. The kidney performs a remarkable range of functions: filtering waste from the blood, regulating fluid, electrolytes and acid-base balance, helping control blood pressure, and producing hormones involved in red blood cell production. Researchers must deliver enough cells throughout the organ and keep them viable long enough to contribute to repair.
"I work on the scale of organs," Dr. Mao says.
At the Organ Rejuvenation Unit, Dr. Mao and colleagues also study livers using the same perfusion platform.
"What we learn in one organ can inform what we do in another," Dr. Mao says. "As each team has a breakthrough, my hope is that we can translate those advances across organ systems and across Mayo Clinic."
From generosity to possibility
The kidney in front of Dr. Mao may never reach a patient, but its story does not end on the perfusion machine. What researchers learn from it could help make more donor organs suitable for transplant and increase the number available to patients.
"What we're doing today in the lab will shape the operating room of tomorrow," Dr. Mao says.
The bigger picture
The work is part of Genesis, Mayo Clinic's initiative to advance new approaches to organ failure across the heart, lungs, liver, kidneys, brain and bone marrow through efforts to prevent damage, repair organs and improve transplantation.
The Organ Rejuvenation Unit was established through a collaboration with the Robert and Arlene Kogod Center on Aging at Mayo Clinic, with support from Mayo Clinic in Florida's executive leadership and Department of Transplantation. Genesis supports the team's work on immunologic cloaking and disease modification.

The post CAR-T cell therapy shows promise for stiff person syndrome appeared first on Mayo Clinic News Network. ]]> A multicenter clinical trial evaluating chimeric antigen receptor-T cell therapy (CAR-T cell therapy) for stiff person syndrome (SPS), a rare autoimmune neurologic disorder, has produced promising results that are already changing lives.
The study, published in JAMA Neurology, found evidence of substantial clinical improvement among participants treated with CAR-T cell therapy. Researchers say the findings warrant further investigation.
Watch: Experimental CAR-T therapy is providing life-changing results for patients with stiff person syndrome
Journalists: Broadcast-quality video (2:49) is in the downloads at the end of this post. Please courtesy: "Mayo Clinic News Network." Read the script.
"What was most striking was the degree of improvement we saw in some patients. With existing treatments, we may be able to improve symptoms, but we very rarely see patients return to their previous level of function. These early results are very encouraging, and the key question now is whether those improvements will be sustained over time," says Anastasia Zekeridou, M.D., Ph.D., a neurologist and researcher at Mayo Clinic.
CAR-T cell therapy reengineers a patient's own immune cells to target other cells contributing to disease. Study participants received a single treatment designed to reset the immune system and reduce symptoms that can profoundly limit daily life.
The rare autoimmune neurologic disease causes progressive muscle stiffness and painful spasms that can make walking, driving, working and socializing increasingly difficult. Mayo Clinic first described the disease in 1956.
When stiff person syndrome narrows daily life
Shari before CAR-T treatment using a walker to navigate a national park.
For Shari St. Germain, SPS didn't just affect her mobility. It narrowed her world.
After developing severe leg cramps and difficulty walking in 2021, she watched familiar routines and favorite activities become sources of anxiety. A sudden noise, a car horn or an unexpected greeting could trigger muscle rigidity and cause her to fall.
"You start losing the ability to go out and be active, to go to concerts, to even walk down the street and have coffee with a friend," she says. "Everything starts to become scary."
As her symptoms worsened, isolation became one of the hardest parts of the disease. By 2024, standard treatments were no longer controlling her symptoms, and she feared she was running out of options.
When the opportunity arose to participate in the CAR-T cell therapy trial, she said yes — hoping it might help future patients, even if it didn't help her.
Shari one week after her CAR-T treatment.
Small steps toward independence
The changes came gradually.
Months after treatment, she began noticing small improvements that added up to something much bigger: independence.
"One day, I got up, and I felt really good. I decided I was going to try walking on the treadmill," she recalled. "I couldn't believe it when I walked for 7 minutes on the treadmill."
Before SPS, Shari routinely walked 7 miles a day. After years of struggling to get off the couch, 7 minutes felt extraordinary.
Jonathan's return to everyday life
Jonathan Walden
For Jonathan Walden, the disease had also taken away much of the life he once knew.
As SPS progressed, walking became difficult. Eventually, he needed help completing basic daily tasks. Some days, he stayed in bed because moving across the room felt impossible.
"My children were helping dress me," Jonathan says. "My life was going nowhere but downhill because of this disease."
The physical limitations were accompanied by a growing sense that his future was slipping away. Today, his abilities have returned.
"I can go to work every single day. I can do everything I did before. I go hunting; I can go fishing," he says. "I have not had one episode since receiving treatment."
For both patients, the value of the trial is measured not only in clinical outcomes but also in moments that many people take for granted: walking without fear, returning to work, spending time with family and reclaiming parts of life that SPS had taken away.
"CAR-T therapy has already transformed the treatment of some cancers, and we are now beginning to see its potential in autoimmune neurologic diseases. The results in stiff person syndrome offer tremendous hope, not only for people living with this disease but potentially for patients with other immune-mediated neurologic conditions where effective treatment options remain limited. There is still much we need to learn, but this opens an exciting new avenue for the field," says Sean Pittock, M.D., chair of the Department of Neurology at Mayo Clinic in Rochester.
Mayo Clinic is one of three participating sites in the trial and played a key role in the research, enrolling patients and providing scientific leadership, including authorship of the publication.

An ex vivo clinical trial would move some drug testing outside the patient’s body, using human cell models and computer-based “digital twins” to guide each round of testing.
The post Could the clinical trial of the future begin before the patient takes the drug? appeared first on Mayo Clinic News Network. ]]> A visual representation of the concept of digital twins (Getty Images).
About a decade ago, Charles Howe, Ph.D., a Mayo Clinic neuroimmunologist, reached a frustrating point in his research on multiple sclerosis.
Much of his earlier work had relied on traditional preclinical models, to study how the immune system damages neurons. Those models could answer important questions, but they did not fully capture the complexities of human biology he was trying to understand.
Charles Howe, Ph.D.,
"Our preclinical models were coming up against a wall," Dr. Howe says. "They just could not capture the right biology."
That realization pushed him to look for better ways to model human disease. His team began collecting patient blood and skin samples and using those cells to grow three-dimensional neural organoids, miniature models of human tissue that Dr. Howe sometimes calls "brains in a dish." These models can preserve important features of an individual patient's biology and give researchers a way to test ideas that could not be explored directly in a person.
As that work evolved, Dr. Howe began thinking beyond individual laboratory models and toward a new way of testing treatments before they ever reach a patient.
His concept, called an ex vivo clinical trial, would move part of the testing outside the patient's body. It would pair living human cell-based models, or "biological avatars," with computer-based "digital twins." Results from laboratory experiments would be used to refine the computer model, and the model's predictions would help guide what researchers test next. The process would continue in a feedback loop, with each round of testing adding new information.
The goal is to learn as much as possible about how a treatment might work and whether it could cause harm before a patient receives it.
How biological avatars and digital twins work together
The term "biological avatar" may sound futuristic, but many of its components already exist. "What's powerful about these models is that they can preserve important aspects of an individual patient's biology,” says Brooke Druliner, Ph.D., director of Mayo Clinic's Human Model Systems Core. "They don't recreate the entire patient, but as we make these systems more complex, we can capture more of the biology that matters in human disease."
Researchers also can place cells in engineered devices known as organ-on-a-chip or microphysiological systems, which can recreate conditions such as blood flow, mechanical forces and interactions among different cell types.
These models give researchers access to living human biology that can be studied and manipulated repeatedly.
A digital twin contributes something different. It is a computer-based model that represents aspects of the patient's biology and physiology using molecular measurements, clinical data and other information. These models can be used to simulate or forecast how the patient might respond to a particular intervention or treatment.
Mayo researchers have already tested that idea in critical care. In one study, they built digital-twin models of patients with sepsis and prospectively compared the models' predicted responses to treatment with what actually happened during the patients' first 24 hours in the intensive care unit.
The power, Dr. Howe says, comes from putting the two together. Researchers can expose the biological avatar to a drug and measure how the cells or tissue respond, including signs of effectiveness or toxicity. Those results are fed into the digital twin along with other information about the patient. The twin can then simulate what might happen under different doses or treatments and help guide what researchers test next.
Each new experiment generates more data, allowing the model to be updated and refined. That continuous updating is what distinguishes a true digital twin from a static computer model.
Could treatments be tested before patients receive them?
Consider a patient with inflammatory bowel disease. Numerous medications are available to treat the condition, but finding the right one can involve a long process of trial and error.
"Start with one. It fails. You give them another one. It fails. You give them another one. It fails," Dr. Howe says.
He imagines a different future. A biopsy taken from the patient could be used to grow intestinal organoids, allowing researchers to test many potential therapies and combinations at the same time.
"You can treat them with every available drug all at once in order to identify one that is likely to work," he says.
Researchers are beginning to build toward that possibility. Mayo researchers routinely grow colonic organoids from tissue donated by patients with ulcerative colitis and have used them to study how the intestinal lining responds to inflammatory signals. But these models capture only part of a patient's biology.
Why drugs fail
The idea could prove useful even before individualized ex vivo trials become part of routine clinical care.
Drug development remains extraordinarily difficult. Fewer than 10% of drugs entering phase 1 clinical trials ultimately reach regulatory approval, and many late-stage failures result from lack of effectiveness or safety concerns.
That gap between traditional preclinical testing and what happens in patients helped motivate Dr. Howe's work. Biological avatars potentially allow researchers to test therapies directly in human-derived tissues earlier in development. Digital twins add the ability to integrate those experimental findings with other data and make predictions about dose, response and toxicity.
Dr. Howe says the repeated back-and-forth between biological avatars and digital twins could help researchers identify weak drug candidates earlier, improve promising ones more quickly and reduce reliance on animal testing. Some of the strongest early evidence comes from cancer, cystic fibrosis and liver toxicity, though the technology is not equally mature across diseases or applications.
The regulatory landscape is evolving as well. The Food and Drug Administration Modernization Act 2.0 of 2022 expanded pathways for using non-animal approaches, including validated human-cell and computational methods, to support drug development.
The trial of the future
The research supports Mayo Clinic's Clinical Impact initiative that aims to reimagine clinical trials so discoveries can reach patients faster. Mayo is pursuing strategies that include simplifying trial operations and using digital technologies, data and platforms to expand and accelerate innovative studies.
Dr. Howe's work also connects with Mayo's broader efforts to build biological and data resources that can be shared across the organization. Those efforts are creating pathways to move patient tissue into organoid and other research workflows, while linking the resulting data with Mayo's Research Data Atlas ecosystem.
But significant hurdles remain. Organoids must be reproducible from one laboratory to another and from one patient to another. Digital twins must be transparent, validated and able to express uncertainty in their predictions. And the entire process must become fast enough to fit the window in which clinicians need to make treatment decisions.
Dr. Howe stresses that these are early days. These systems are not yet ready to guide routine patient care, but he can envision where the field could lead.
In the future, he says, clinical trials could begin by screening a therapy against an avatar that reflects the patient's biology. Researchers could look for signs that the treatment will work, as well as potential toxicities, before the therapy is given.
"Clinical trials are never going to go away," Dr. Howe says. "But the more we can learn before a therapy reaches the patient, the better chance we have of choosing something that will work."
